video.title: Shoulder Adduction Unlocks the Tennis Forehand

classification.reason: The coach explains how shoulder adduction serves as the final link in the forehand kinetic chain, how to set up the contact zone, and how to adjust body positioning.

problem.title_as_question: How does shoulder adduction work in the tennis forehand and how do you harness it?
problem.definition: Shoulder adduction naturally pulls the arm across the body and closes the face sideways, so players must position their body and contact zone such that adduction drives back-to-front toward the target with a stable string angle.
problem.target_player: 3.0, 2.5, 3.5, or even 4.0/4.5 players who want to make clean and consistent contact without missing or framing

symptoms.description: The ball flies sideways or down when swinging across the body.
The racket face closes completely or turns over excessively (e.g. 100 degrees) through contact.
Shanking or framing the ball off the frame when the ball spacing is misjudged.

causes.statement: Natural shoulder adduction pulls the arm horizontally across the body rather than straight back-to-front unless aligned into a proper orientation.
Shoulder adduction naturally couples with internal shoulder rotation, causing the hand and racket face to turn over completely.
The player fails to probe and position the body relative to the ball, leaving the ball too far, too close, or too behind the contact zone.
The hitting elbow remains trapped behind the plane of the hips instead of swinging forward past the hips before adduction fires.

angles.summary: Shoulder adduction is the final link in the kinetic chain and naturally couples with internal shoulder rotation.
Players should not push straight forward into the shot; they must pull across the body but orient the swing so the pull moves back to front at contact.
A fault-tolerant contact zone defines the window from where the elbow clears the hips to where the shoulder is fully adducted.
Adjusting hip tilt and torso posture on low and high balls allows the player to maintain the exact same shoulder adduction path.

solutions.summary: Pull across your body rather than pushing forward, setting up the swing so the cross-body pull travels back to front through contact.
Hold the racket and freeze at the contact window to check that strings remain at a stable, slight downward angle rather than completely turning over.
solutions.external_goal: Check racket strings on a slight downward angle

solutions.summary: Ensure the hitting elbow passes forward past the plane of the hips before initiating the final cross-body shoulder adduction.
Probe low balls by tilting the hips and torso rather than dropping the isolated arm, keeping the shoulder adduction slot constant.
Once you feel the consistent string angle through adduction in shadow swings, look in front and adjust footwork to position the incoming ball into that exact hitting slot.
solutions.external_goal: Set the ball up in the visual hitting slot
